review.title: Nhận xét bài viết trên lớp
paragraphs: There is an opinion that school should reward students who has excellent academic performance; however, some people believe that improved students have the right to rewarded. From my perspective, there are strong cases to be made for both sides of the argument.

On the one hand, rewarding students who show the best academic results is undeniable. Students have diligently applied themselves to their studies and they deserve their praises and privileges. This may encourage these students and others to study harder to win the rewards, from that, they would propel towards overall academic gains. Moreover, this kind of competition has seen in almost every aspect of life where only the best individuals are rewarded. From a long time ago, students are used to this reality and thrive in the face of fierce competition and it enable them to achieve success in later life.

On the other hand, students who showly effort in learning progress are equally rewarding. Only a few smart students can come first and receive the rewards, thus cause others to think that their effort is futile because they can not surpass those outstanding individuals. They would prone to feeling overwhelmed and disheartened, thus gradually lose the incentive to study. Because of that, emphasizing improvements is also crucial in order to encourage all students to be diligent in their studies and help students to understand that they need to constantly improve themselves, irrespective of how well they have been or are performing. The constant desire to outdo themselves, even benefit themselves more than the competitive determination to win against the others.
In conclusion, I am firmly convinced that both kinds of students should be reward no matter what fields they have succeeded in.

review.title: Nhận xét bài viết trên lớp
paragraphs: There is an argument that dangerous sports should be prohibited by law while the others think that individuals should be free to take part. I am personally of the latter school of thought, provided that certain conditions are met.

Admittedly, one might argue that dangerous sports should be prohibited because even a minor minor can lead to the death of a participant. I believe that this prohibition is impractical. First of all, this kind of sport is often take place in remote locations, say, mountain cliffs, where is minimal surveillance and control. Moreover, it is unrealistic that a police officer can follow every individuals. Because of that, a prohibition exist only a paper, it can drive practice underground which harder to ensure basic safety standards.

However, people should be permitted to do any sports, as long as they understand risks and receive sufficient training. For example, deep-ocean diving, ought to join reputable club, where is appropriate equipment + qualified supervision. New players can be accompanied by an expert to taught to what to do when accidents occur in order to recognise dangers and respond appropriately. Finally proper training and necessary precautions can safer participation; because no activity is entirely risk-free.
In conclusion, banning is neither practical nor effective. People have freedom to choose, under strict condition of training and awareness and that is a more realistic approach.

paragraphs: There is an argument that dangerous sports should be prohibited by law while the others think that individuals should be free to take part. I am personally of the latter school of thought, provided that certain conditions are met.

Admittedly, one might argue that dangerous sports should be prohibited. This is because even a minor error can lead to the death of a participant. However, I believe that this prohibition is impractical. First of all, this kind of sport often takes place in remote locations, say, mountain cliffs, where surveillance and control are minimal. Moreover, it is unrealistic that a police officer can follow every individual. As a result, a prohibition may exist only on paper and may drive the practice underground, making it harder to ensure basic safety standards.

Moreover, people should be permitted to do any sports, as long as they understand risks and receive sufficient training. For example, people who try deep-ocean diving ought to join a reputable club that provides appropriate equipment and qualified supervision. New players can be accompanied by an expert and taught what to do when accidents occur in order to recognise dangers and respond appropriately. Finally, proper training and necessary precautions can make participation safer, although no activity is entirely risk-free.
In conclusion, banning is neither practical nor effective. People have freedom to choose under strict conditions of training and awareness; this is a more realistic approach.

Admittedly, one might opponents of a trial and error approach often emphasize this view three reasons. Parents can prevent as most mistakes as avoidable as they can. For example, children do not need to get hurt by knives, fire, electricity are unnecessary to get hurt to learn to be careful. Moreover, they can shield children from harm, forestall mistakes and fulfil this duty. Finally, with pre-emptively help children, adults can have peace of mind because they do their best to protect and raise their child.

However, those on the other side have their own valid reasoning. Parent cannot be around all the time and children need to experiment with new things, so making mistakes is inevitable. Mistakes also contain invaluable lessons, which can help children in good stead in later stages of life. By learn from mistakes, children might be shielded from everything, thereby, growing up overdependent on others and have undesirable trait.

Overall, it seem to me that allowing children to learn from mistakes is a way to prepare for the future. Provided that parents provide guidance in important matters, they can help their children avoid making mistakes that may derail their future.

paragraphs: Some people believe that children have the right to learn through trial and error, whereas others argue that adults should help them avoid mistakes. From my perspective, the freedom for children to make mistakes should be encouraged, provided that the errors do not involve serious danger.

Admittedly, opponents of the trial-and-error approach often emphasise three reasons for their view. Parents can prevent many avoidable mistakes. For example, children do not need to get hurt by knives, fire or electricity to learn to be careful. Moreover, parents can shield children from harm, forestall mistakes and fulfil this duty. Finally, by helping children pre-emptively, adults can have peace of mind since they have done their best to protect and raise their child.

However, those who favour children's freedom to make mistakes have their own valid reasoning. Parents cannot be around their children all the time, and children need to experiment with new things; consequently, making some mistakes is inevitable. Mistakes also contain invaluable lessons, which can stand children in good stead later in life. If children are shielded from everything, they may grow up overdependent on others and develop an undesirable trait.

Overall, it seems to me that allowing children to learn from mistakes is a way to prepare for the future. Provided that parents provide guidance in important matters, they can help their children avoid making mistakes that may derail their future.

Overall, gas emissions rose throughout the period and became the highest of the three from 2000 onwards. Coal emissions fell steadily from the highest level at the start to the lowest level at the end. Oil emissions also declined overall, although they rose briefly between 1995 and 2000.

In 1990, coal produced approximately 310 million tons of emissions, compared with around 270 million tons from oil and 220 million tons from gas. By 1995, gas had risen to about 270 million tons, while coal had declined to roughly 280 million tons and oil to around 240 million tons. In 2000, gas reached about 300 million tons and overtook both other sources. At that point, oil emitted around 260 million tons and coal about 250 million tons.

From 2000 onwards, gas emissions continued to rise, reaching approximately 320 million tons by 2010. Over the same period, oil declined to roughly 210 million tons and coal fell to around 190 million tons. Coal was therefore the smallest source of the three at the end of the period.

paragraphs.text: Some people believe that history is one of the most important subjects at school, while others give greater priority to science and technology in the modern world. I believe that both areas have value because they prepare students for different parts of life.

On the one hand, history helps students understand how past events shaped their country and its people. A lesson about a period of conflict, for example, can show them why earlier generations made difficult choices and what those choices cost. This knowledge can deepen their appreciation of cultural traditions and help them think critically about present-day issues. Historical study also asks students to compare sources rather than accept a single account without evidence. These abilities are useful well beyond a history classroom.

On the other hand, science and technology give students tools for solving practical problems. Science lessons can teach them how to test explanations and understand natural processes. Technology classes help them use computers and other devices that are now common in many occupations. For example, students who learn to analyse data may later work on better transport systems or medical research. A strong grounding in these subjects can therefore create more career opportunities and help communities respond to new challenges. This does not make history unnecessary; the two fields develop different strengths.

In conclusion, history supports cultural understanding and careful judgment, whereas science and technology support practical problem solving and future work. Schools should teach all three subjects well so that students can use these complementary forms of knowledge.
